iss/sibal.q1:
1 · Does it burn here?

BURNS · ✅ within tested conditions

In Saffire it burned completely with 21.5–22.1 % O₂ and air at 20 cm/s. More oxygen only makes it worse.

Saffire-II · Urban et al. 2024 (Saffire VI)
iss/sibal.q3:
3 · What to do?

🔥 ISS · in orbit · Cotton–fiberglass fabric (SIBAL) · 21.0 % O₂

🧑‍✈️ Commander🧑‍🚀 Crew member 2📡 Ground control
BeforepreventKnow where the cotton–fiberglass fabric (SIBAL) is: at this O₂ it can burn.Saffire-II · Urban et al. 2024 (Saffire VI)Check the smoke detector and the CO sensor. Ventilation must be on: without it smoke never reaches the detector.Meyer 2016Confirm O₂ and pressure are within what this vehicle is certified for.Hirsch et al. 2009
T+1:00warningCall "fire!" and locate the source. In microgravity the flame is blue and almost invisible: look for the glow and the smoke hugging the source.Meyer 2016Masks (PBA) on for both.Saffire, ICES 2024Track CO and O₂ live and open the fire emergency procedure.Urban et al. 2016
T+2:00actSwitch off ventilation and power in the area. Without airflow, the flame starves.BASS-II · Sacksteder y T'ien 1993CO₂ extinguisher ready. If it is still burning after 30 s: fire at the base of the flame, from the side the air was coming from. Never helium.FLEX · Takahashi et al. 2001Confirm power is off and count the time to 425 ppm CO.Saffire, ICES 2024
T+2:30confirmCheck it is out: in microgravity the flame is hard to see; look for any glow or smoke.Watch for re-ignition: an almost invisible cool flame can continue after it goes out.FLEXKeep tracking CO with the crew still masked.Saffire, ICES 2024
Afterclean the airTurn ventilation back on with the filters to clean the air: without it, acid gases take much longer to clear.Niehaus et al. 2026Keep masks on until CO is below the limit.Saffire, ICES 2024Record what burned and check the rest of the cotton–fiberglass fabric (SIBAL) on board.

iss/sibal.q5:
Where every number comes from

7 of 13 numbers come from NASA (54 %)

  • measured (PSI) Burned / did not ignite at 21.5–22.1 % O₂ Saffire-II · Urban et al. 2024 (Saffire VI)
  • measured (PSI) Flame spread 0.6–2.6 mm/s (air at 20 cm/s) Saffire-II
  • measured (PSI) Burning faster with more O₂: ×1.00 (heptane droplets) FLEX
  • our assumption Solids speed up with O₂ like the FLEX droplets (analogy)
  • NASA literature Saffire fires: 1.5–3.2 kW in 17–19 m³ Urban et al. 2024 (Saffire VI)
  • NASA literature Far-field CO after a Saffire fire: 1,390–2,360 ppm; 1-hour limit 425 ppm Saffire, ICES 2024
  • our assumption CO grows in proportion to burned area, evenly while it burns
  • our assumption Well-mixed cabin air with no filters (conservative)
  • NASA literature Volume 388 m³ · 21.0 % O₂ · 1.00 atm Urban et al. 2016 · Hirsch et al. 2009
  • our assumption Smoke detector 3 m away, 30 s for the smoke to build up; buoyant plume 50 cm/s at 1 g
  • our assumption CO alarm at 50 ppm (5 ppm with CPM)
  • our assumption After switching off ventilation the flame dies in 30 s; extinguisher takes 60 s
  • NASA literature High O₂ (≥ 30 %): flame survives without ventilation BRE
iss/sibal.q6:
Model check

Each fit is checked by hiding one test at a time, predicting it with the rest and measuring the error (leave-one-out).

ModelDataMean error
O₂ at which PMMA plates go outBASS-II · 16± 1,3 points O₂
O₂ at which PMMA rods go outBASS-II · 25± 1,4 points O₂
🧠 Chance of burning (Super-Intelligence, logistic regression)BASS-II · 82± 1,4 points O₂
Heptane droplet burning rate (d² law)FLEX · 41± 0,105 mm²/s (of ~0,57)
Methanol droplet burning rateFLEX · 53± 0,038 mm²/s (of ~0,47)

Not validated yet: CO growth and detection times in a real crewed cabin (no open data exists). NASA validated a full CFD model of Saffire (Niehaus et al. 2026); ours is the fast version for decisions.

Saffire-II · Urban et al. 2024 (Saffire VI)

🧪 To stop extrapolating, NASA would need this test: cotton–fiberglass fabric (SIBAL) at 26.5 % O₂ and 0.69 atm, in microgravity. PSI has 10 tested conditions nearby (±2.5 O₂ points, ±0.1 atm) in ACME BRE, FLEX. See the gap map → · How we fill the gaps →

reentry/sibal.q5:
Where every number comes from

7 of 13 numbers come from NASA (54 %)

  • measured (PSI) Burned / did not ignite at 21.5–22.1 % O₂ Saffire-II · Urban et al. 2024 (Saffire VI)
  • measured (PSI) Flame spread 0.6–2.6 mm/s (air at 20 cm/s) Saffire-II
  • measured (PSI) Burning faster with more O₂: ×1.15 (heptane droplets) FLEX
  • our assumption Solids speed up with O₂ like the FLEX droplets (analogy)
  • NASA literature Saffire fires: 1.5–3.2 kW in 17–19 m³ Urban et al. 2024 (Saffire VI)
  • NASA literature Far-field CO after a Saffire fire: 1,390–2,360 ppm; 1-hour limit 425 ppm Saffire, ICES 2024
  • our assumption CO grows in proportion to burned area, evenly while it burns
  • our assumption Well-mixed cabin air with no filters (conservative)
  • NASA literature Volume 9 m³ · 25.6 % O₂ · 1.00 atm Urban et al. 2016 · Hirsch et al. 2009
  • our assumption Smoke detector 3 m away, 30 s for the smoke to build up; buoyant plume 50 cm/s at 1 g
  • our assumption CO alarm at 50 ppm (5 ppm with CPM)
  • our assumption After switching off ventilation the flame dies in 30 s; extinguisher takes 60 s
  • NASA literature High O₂ (≥ 30 %): flame survives without ventilation BRE

1 · Does it burn here?

UNTESTED · ⚠️ extrapolated

In Saffire-II it did not ignite with ~22.1 % O₂ and air at 20 cm/s. Here there is more oxygen or gravity than tested: NASA warns that materials that do not burn on Earth can burn in exploration atmospheres (Abney et al. 2026).

Partial gravity can be the worst case ("Goldilocks"): little flow to cool the flame, enough to feed it (Zayac et al. 2024 · Sacksteder y T'ien 1993). Result extrapolated.

BASS-II and Saffire were at ~1 atm. NASA rates materials mainly by O₂ concentration (Hirsch et al. 2009), so lower pressure is treated as a caveat, not a fix.

Saffire-II

PSI has 3 tested conditions nearby (±2.5 O₂ points, ±0.1 atm) in ACME CFI-G, ACME/Flame Design, FLEX-2; PSI investigations are in microgravity or on the ground, none at partial gravity. panel: NASA SPACE APPS CHALLENGE 2026 · FLAME IN FREEFALL What would a fire do in your spacecraft? Astale turns NASA microgravity combustion experiments into answers a crew can act on: does it burn here?, how much time is there? and what does each person do?, on the ISS, Orion or a base on the Moon or Mars. And it answers the challenge goals one by one. 🔥 Try the Fire Twin ↓ Flame on the ISS: the yellow is glowing soot · NASA 🔥 Fire Twin Simulate a fire in your vehicle 🧠 Model Train and predict on NASA data 🔭 Investigations The most relevant for your mission 📊 Data Downloads, gaps and validation 🛠️ Design Rules for equipment and controls 🌍 On Earth What is useful here ℹ️ About Team, limits and method What the "Flame in Freefall" challenge asks, and where it is 1 Identify the investigations most relevant to the safety of inhabited environments → Investigations 2 Extract data useful for predictive flammability and fire models → Data 3 Highlight what helps design next-generation equipment and controls → Design 4 Connect it to applications on Earth → On Earth ★ Super-Intelligence-powered: our own model trained on NASA data → Model

🧠 Our predictive model: trained right here on NASA data, no API An ensemble of XGBoost, CatBoost, random forest and linear regression is trained in your browser on the 257 fuel droplets that burned on the ISS (FLEX), alongside baseline models. They are compared with cross-validation, you see which variables decide, and you can predict. No pay-per-use, same result every time. How fast does it burn? Burning rate K (mm²/s) Does the flame go out by itself? Before the fuel is used up (yes / no) 1 · Train and compare Model Fit (R²) Mean error Linear / logistic regression top score 0.70 ±0.048 mm²/s Weighted ensemble: XGBoost 40 % + CatBoost 40 % + forest 10 % + linear 10 % used to predict 0.70 ±0.049 mm²/s CatBoost (algorithm, symmetric trees) 0.69 ±0.050 mm²/s Random forest (120 trees) 0.67 ±0.051 mm²/s XGBoost (algorithm, 300 trees) 0.67 ±0.052 mm²/s Nearest neighbours (k = 7) 0.67 ±0.053 mm²/s The ensemble used to predict explains 70 % of the differences between droplets it never saw; the best single model, 70 %. The simplest model wins: with 257 droplets, a complex one adds nothing. 2 · Which variables matter most Oxygen Helium in the air Droplet size CO₂ in the air Fuel (heptane / methanol) Pressure How much worse the model gets when that variable is shuffled (on unseen droplets). Oxygen decides the most, as combustion physics says. 3 · Predict Heptane Methanol Oxygen 21.0 % Pressure 1.00 atm CO₂ in the air 0 % Helium in the air 0 % Droplet size 2.5 mm Burning rate 0.58 mm²/s ± 0.08 Goes out by itself 17 % probability A 2.5 mm droplet would take about 10.7 s to burn completely (d² law). Models: Weighted ensemble: XGBoost 40 % + CatBoost 40 % + forest 10 % + linear 10 % · Weighted ensemble: XGBoost 40 % + CatBoost 40 % + forest 10 % + linear 10 %. The ± is the disagreement among the forest’s 120 trees. 📄 Model documentation What it predicts Two things about a fuel droplet burning in microgravity: how fast it is consumed (d²-law constant, K in mm²/s) and whether the flame goes out by itself before the fuel runs out. The first feeds the fire speed of the Fire Twin; the second tells when an inert gas (CO₂, helium) is enough to put it out. Data 257 heptane and methanol droplets burned on the ISS in the FLEX experiment (NASA PSI-69, CC0 licence), with 12–34 % oxygen, 0.2–3 atm, added CO₂ and helium and 1.1–4.7 mm droplets. 6 input variables. Download the CSV. Models XGBoost — second-order boosting with regularisation (λ = 1), 300 trees of depth 4, η = 0.05, 80 % of rows and columns per tree. Chen & Guestrin, KDD 2016. CatBoost — boosting with symmetric trees (same question across a whole level), 300 trees of depth 4, λ = 3. Prokhorenkova et al., NeurIPS 2018. Random forest — 120 trees, 60 % of the variables at each split. Breiman, 2001. Linear / logistic and neighbours (k = 7) as baselines. Ensemble — weighted mean: XGBoost 40 %, CatBoost 40 %, forest 10 %, linear 10 % (team decision: more weight to boosting). It is the one used to predict. Equal weights scored slightly higher (R² 0.71 and 86 %), and we say so. How it is validated 5-fold cross-validation with a fixed seed: each droplet is predicted by a model trained without it. Regression: R² and mean absolute error. Classification: accuracy and AUC, compared with always giving the most common answer. Variable importance by permutation, on unseen droplets. How it is built All in JavaScript, in the browser (ml/index.js): no libraries, no server and no paid API. The XGBoost and CatBoost algorithms are written here following their papers (32-bin histograms, like the original libraries); they are not the official libraries. With the same seed, the numbers are always the same. Limits Only droplets of two fuels in microgravity: not fabrics or plastics (BASS-II and Saffire cover those in the Fire Twin). Outside the tested ranges the prediction is flagged as extrapolated. Little data: complex models barely beat linear regression, and that is a result too. Model card · data: 257 FLEX droplets on the ISS (NASA PSI-69, CC0), downloadable above · variables: fuel, oxygen, pressure, CO₂, helium and droplet size · validation: 5 folds, each droplet is predicted by a model that never saw it · limits: only heptane and methanol droplets in microgravity; outside the tested ranges the prediction is flagged as extrapolated.

1 Identify the investigations most relevant to the safety of inhabited environments The 24 PSI combustion investigations ranked 0–100 for the mission you choose: what the challenge asks (40) + the safety pillar (40) + whether there are tests in that atmosphere (20). Mission ISS / spacecraft in orbit Spacecraft on an asteroid Orion (Artemis) EVA preparation atmosphere Lunar base Pressurised rover Exploration / Mars Spacesuit (reference) Pillar All Prevention Detection Suppression Modelling O₂ 30 % · 10.2 psi — According to the challenge: "30 % or more O₂ at 10.2 psi or less". +40 % more oxygen than on Earth. FLEX PSI-69 · liquid · tested conditions Discovered "cool flames": heptane keeps reacting after the visible flame goes out. Includes tests in lunar-base conditions (30–34 % O₂ at ~0.7 atm). 100 ACME BRE PSI-20 · gas · tested conditions ⚠️ Key: at high O₂ the flame kept burning WITHOUT ventilation. Shutting off ventilation is an established step in fighting spacecraft fires: on the Moon it may not be enough. 96 BASS PSI-26 · solid · no tests like this Starting hypothesis: with ventilation, a material burns in microgravity as well as or BETTER than on Earth. Calls into question NASA's standard test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1), which is carried out under gravity. 80 SAFFIRE-I PSI-98 · solid · no tests like this Real scale: how a fire grows and what it does to the spacecraft's O₂, CO₂, pressure and temperature. 80 BASS-II PSI-25 · solid · no tests like this The most complete set of solid flammability limits in microgravity… but always at 1 atm and with O₂ ≤ 22 %. Nothing in a lunar atmosphere. 80 SAFFIRE-III PSI-100 · solid · no tests like this Repeatability and the effect of air velocity on a large fire. 76 SAME PSI-102 · smoke · no tests like this Tells us whether current smoke detectors "see" microgravity smoke. Basis for the detector on future spacecraft. 76 SAME-R PSI-101 · smoke · no tests like this More particle-size data; corrected the sample contamination problems of SAME. 72 See all 24 with filters and full cards →

PSI-69 What is not validated yet CO growth in a crewed cabin and detection time: only two large fires have been measured (Saffire VI) and the model was calibrated with them, so they cannot also be used to check it. NASA has a detailed (CFD) model of those fires, Niehaus 2026: that is the next comparison. Scientific review pending: José Luis Endrino and Prof. Saurav Goel. 🧩 How we fill the gaps: what Astale does where there are no tests The Moon, Mars and atmospheres above 23 % O₂ have almost no tests. Astale neither stays silent nor makes things up: it answers with these four rules and flags it. 1 📏 Bracket between what was measured There are no partial-gravity tests, but there are in microgravity (BASS-II, ISS) and with Earth gravity. The oxygen limit on the Moon or Mars is taken between the two, keeping the more dangerous one. 2 🛡️ When in doubt, the most dangerous A material with no tests at that oxygen is treated as burning, never as safe. Below the tested pressure, the last measured value is used, which gives a slightly faster fire. And in partial gravity we do not assume cutting ventilation puts the fire out (BRE saw flames keep going without it at high O₂). 3 📚 Physics and NASA literature CO is scaled by cabin volume from the real Saffire VI fires; smoke rises according to gravity. Zayac 2024 warns that partial gravity can be the worst case: too little flow to cool the flame, enough to feed it. 4 🔦 Say so and point to the gap Every such result carries ⚠️ "extrapolated", the Fire Twin says which NASA test is missing and how many similar ones PSI has, and the gap map above shows where there is no data. We do not invent numbers that look measured. 🌑 Example: a fabric catches fire on the lunar base (34 % O₂ · 0.56 atm · 0.16 g · 30 m³) Does it burn? Yes ⚠️ extrapolated: the fabric was only tested up to 22 % O₂ and in microgravity (Saffire-II). How much time? CO would reach the 1-hour limit in 42 s (worst case), scaling Saffire VI to 30 m³. What to do? Extinguisher now, without waiting for cutting the air to put it out, and prepare to evacuate the habitat (BRE, Zayac 2024). What is missing? A fabric test at 34 % O₂, 0.56 atm and 0.16 g. PSI has 11 tested conditions nearby, and none at partial gravity: that is what LUCI and FM2 will measure. See it in the Fire Twin →

3 Highlight what helps design next-generation equipment and controls Six design rules, each with its number, its source and how much we trust it. For vehicle and habitat engineers, not for the crew (the crew part is the Fire Twin action card). 13.6 % 🧪 Test materials in microgravity, with airflow BASS-II acrylic rods kept burning down to 13.6 % O₂ in 0 g with slow air. The standard test (NASA-STD-6001, under gravity) may not be conservative. Nomex and thick silicone did not spread in Saffire-II (21.5–22 % O₂): good candidates, but no data at higher oxygen. high confidence · measured BASS-II · BASS · Saffire-II 26.5–34 % 🌀 Fast ventilation shut-off… not enough with high O₂ In 0 g, without airflow the flame starves near its limit: that is why cutting ventilation is the first step on the ISS. But in BRE, with exploration atmospheres (26.5 % at 10.2 psi and 34 % at 8.2 psi) the flame kept burning without ventilation: those vehicles need an extinguisher as well as the shut-off. medium confidence · measured + calculation BRE · Sacksteder & T'ien 1993 +9 % 💧 More O₂ and lower pressure = faster burning With the FLEX fit (K = 0.013 + 1.842·O₂ + 0.170·p, ±0.11 mm²/s), a heptane droplet burns 9 % faster in the EVA-prep atmosphere (26.5 %, 0.69 atm) than in air. In the Mars one (34 %, 0.56 atm) it would be 29 %, but that is extrapolation. Equipment response times must shrink on those missions. medium confidence · measured + calculation FLEX · FLEX-2 ×6–12 😷 CO sensor and masks from the first alarm Saffire VI (1.5–3.2 kW) left 1,390–2,360 ppm of CO in a 17–19 m³ Cygnus. The same fire in a 9 m³ capsule like Orion would give 2,626–4,982 ppm: 6 to 12 times the 1-hour limit (425 ppm). In small vehicles, smoke is the danger even if the fire goes out quickly. medium confidence · measured + calculation Saffire VI (Urban 2024) · Saffire, ICES 2024 3–14 min 📡 Detectors tested with microgravity smoke In Saffire-II the flame advanced 0.6–2.6 mm/s: a 50 cm fabric takes 3–14 minutes to burn completely. There is time, but only with early detection. SAME and SAME-R measured that 0 g smoke has a different particle size: detectors must be calibrated with that smoke, and tell it apart from dust (DAFT; the Moon will have plenty). medium confidence · measured + calculation SAME · SAME-R · DAFT · Saffire-II cool flame 🔁 Watch for re-ignition after extinguishing FLEX discovered "cool flames": the fuel keeps reacting, with no visible flame, after going out. CFI and ACME CFI-G study it. A fire that looks out can flare up again: the controls must keep measuring temperature and gases for a while afterwards, not just look. low confidence · qualitative FLEX · CFI · ACME CFI-G

4 Connect it to applications on Earth What we learn from a fire in space also saves lives here. 🌍 Water-mist extinguishers Very fine water droplets put fires out with little water and without damaging equipment. NASA's Water Mist program (Colorado School of Mines, STS-107) studied in microgravity which droplet size best stops a flame front; FLEX adds 258 measured droplets for evaporation models. Useful in server rooms, ships, trains and museums. Water Mist (NASA) · FLEX · Photo: NASA 🌍 Smarter smoke detectors SAME measured the size of smoke particles from spacecraft materials. That knowledge feeds detectors that warn earlier with fewer false alarms, telling smoke from dust or steam (DAFT): kitchens, hospitals, aircraft. SAME · DAFT · Photo: NASA 🌍 Firefighters in enclosed spaces Saffire is the only test of a large fire in a real spacecraft: how it grows with slow air, how much CO it leaves and how much the pressure rises. Those are the same questions as a fire in a tunnel, a submarine or a poorly ventilated basement, where smoke kills before flames. Saffire · Saffire VI · Photo: NASA 🌍 Oxygen-enriched rooms Hospitals, hyperbaric chambers and patients on home oxygen: with more O₂ everything burns faster and sootier (the yellow flame in the photo). BRE showed that with high O₂ the flame keeps going without ventilation: cutting the air is not enough, the oxygen must be cut. BRE · BASS-II · Photo: NASA

ℹ️ Why fire is different in space, and who we are The problem, the limits of the dashboard, the team and how we use Super-Intelligence. The same candle on Earth (left) and in microgravity (right) · NASA 🔵 Flames are round and faint Without buoyancy, oxygen only arrives by diffusion or ventilation: flames turn blue, round and sometimes almost invisible. 💨 Smoke does not rise It stays near the source and only travels with the ventilation. Switch the fans off and the smoke detector may never see it. 🫁 The air is all there is No windows to open: CO builds up in the cabin, and in a small capsule far sooner than in a station. 🧪 More oxygen ahead Exploration vehicles plan lower pressure and more oxygen (up to 34 %). Materials that are safe on Earth can burn there. What it does not do (yet) It is a fast decision model, not a full simulation: for that NASA uses CFD models of Saffire (Niehaus 2026). CO growth and detection times are not validated in a crewed cabin: no open data exists. Partial gravity (Moon, Mars) and atmospheres above 23 % O₂ are extrapolated, and always flagged. Lithium batteries and propellants are out of scope. Use of Super-Intelligence Extracted knowledge: Claude read the 24 PSI combustion investigations and drafted summaries, classification and safety reading; the team reviewed them and the official data are untouched. Our own models: a weighted ensemble of XGBoost, CatBoost, random forest and linear regression trained in the browser on 257 FLEX droplets (burning rate, R² 0.70; whether the flame goes out by itself, 84 % accuracy, AUC 0.89) and a logistic regression on 82 BASS-II observations (±1.4 O₂ points). No API. Expert system: the action-card rules, each with its NASA source. Ask the dashboard: Claude answers only from the data on this page and cites the source.
